chapters.title: Chapter 5: Putting Sector Rotation Into Practice

lessons.title: Choosing the Vehicle: Sectoral Index Funds, ETFs, Active Sector Funds, or Stocks

body.text: A good sector call can be ruined by the wrong vehicle. Costs, concentration, liquidity, and taxes decide how much of a sector's return actually reaches your pocket.

children.text: Chapters 1 to 4 were about deciding which sectors to favour and when. Chapter 5 is about acting on those decisions sensibly. This lesson compares the four ways an Indian investor can express a sector view: sectoral index funds, sector ETFs, actively managed sector and thematic funds, and individual stocks. None is best for everyone. The right choice depends on how you invest, how often you expect to switch, and how much concentration risk you can live with.

children.text: Sectoral Index Funds and ETFs

markDefs.definition: The gap between a passive fund's return and its index's return over a period, caused mainly by expenses, cash holdings, and trading costs. Tracking error measures how much that gap varies over time.

children.text: Passive vehicles simply hold the stocks in a sector index, such as the Nifty Bank or Nifty IT, in the same weights. You get the sector's return, minus costs and a small
tracking difference
. Because nobody is picking stocks, costs are low, and there is no risk of a manager making a bad call.

body.title: Index Fund vs ETF for the Same Sector

columns.label: Sector index fund
points: Bought and sold at end-of-day NAV, directly with the fund house
No demat account needed; SIPs are easy to set up
No bid-ask spread or reliance on exchange liquidity
Expense ratio usually a little higher than the equivalent ETF
Better suited to regular investing and gradual switching

columns.label: Sector ETF
points: Bought and sold on NSE or BSE during market hours at the traded price
Needs a demat and trading account; brokerage applies
Traded price can drift from the fund's indicative NAV if trading volume is thin
Often the lowest expense ratio available
Better suited to lump sums and precise timing of entries and exits

body.text: Check an ETF's trading volume and bid-ask spread before buying. Many Indian sector ETFs trade thinly. If the spread is wide, or the traded price is well above the indicative NAV shown on the exchange website, you can lose more on a single trade than a whole year of expense ratio saves you.

children.text: Active Sector and Thematic Funds

Active sector funds hand the stock selection within the sector to a fund manager. Under SEBI's categorisation rules, a sectoral or thematic fund must invest at least 80% of its total assets in equities of its chosen sector or theme. A circular issued on 26 February 2026 separated sectoral funds, which focus on one sector, from thematic funds, which can span two or more sectors under a theme, and limited their portfolio overlap with other equity schemes to 50%, with existing schemes given three years to comply.

columns.label: Case for active
points: A manager can underweight a dominant stock that looks overvalued
Can hold smaller companies outside the index that benefit from the theme
Up to 20% of assets can sit outside the sector or theme
Useful where no suitable index product exists

columns.label: Case for passive
points: Lower costs compound in your favour every year
You get exactly the sector exposure your rotation view calls for
No manager risk layered on top of sector risk
Easier to measure with the relative strength tools from Lesson 4.4

body.text: Watch the calendar of new fund launches. Fund houses tend to launch thematic funds in whatever theme has recently performed best, because that is what investors want to buy. In August 2024, about 74% of all new fund offer money went into thematic funds. Heavy launch activity in a theme is usually a sign that a large part of the move has already happened, the late signal from Lesson 4.2.

children.text: Also check the exit load before investing. Many active equity funds charge an exit load, commonly 1%, if you redeem within a set period. That period varies by scheme and is changed from time to time; one large fund house cut it from a year to a month for several schemes from April 2026. A rotation strategy that switches often can run into exit loads repeatedly.
Direct Stocks

Buying stocks lets you avoid annual fund fees and choose exactly which companies to own. But sector indices are often dominated by a handful of names, so building a genuinely representative sector portfolio takes more stocks and more research than it seems.

In July 2026, TCS alone made up 35.4% of the Nifty IT index, and the top three stocks together 68.75%. A "sector bet" on IT through the index was, in large part, a bet on three companies. If you buy two IT stocks directly, you might end up far more or far less exposed to the sector trend than you intended.
Direct stocks make sense when you have a genuine company-level view, not just a sector view.
They add company-specific risk: a single bad quarter, management change, or regulatory action can swamp the sector trend.
They demand ongoing research and monitoring, which many investors underestimate.
The Cost of Switching: Expenses and Taxes
Sector rotation means switching, and every switch has costs. Two matter most: the annual expense drag of the vehicle, and the capital gains tax triggered each time you sell at a profit.

body.title: Measure the Expense Drag
body.prompt: You invest ₹5 lakh in a sector for 5 years, and the sector returns 12% a year before costs. How much more would you have after 5 years with a fund charging 0.30% a year than with one charging 1.00%? Give the answer in rupees, rounded to the nearest ₹1,000.
body.explanation: At 0.30%, ₹5 lakh grows to about ₹8,69,432; at 1.00%, to about ₹8,42,529. The difference is about ₹26,903, from a gap of just 0.70 percentage points a year. The expense figures here are illustrative; check each scheme's actual expense ratio, which is now disclosed as a base expense ratio plus separately shown costs and levies.

children.text: Capital Gains Tax on Every Switch

Selling a sector fund, ETF, or stock at a profit to move into another sector is a taxable transfer. For listed equity shares and equity-oriented mutual funds, including equity ETFs, the rules from 23 July 2024, carried into the Income-tax Act, 2025, are summarised below.

body.caption: Equity capital gains tax (plus applicable surcharge and cess)

cells: 12 months or less
Short-term capital gain
Section 196 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 111A of the Income-tax Act, 1961)
More than 12 months
Long-term capital gain
12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh in a financial year
Section 198 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 112A of the Income-tax Act, 1961)

body.title: Timing a Switch
body.prompt: You bought a sector ETF for ₹3.5 lakh, and it is now worth ₹5 lakh, a gain of ₹1.5 lakh. Your rotation signal says switch. If you sell after 10 months, the gain is short-term. If you wait until after 12 months and the value is unchanged, it is long-term, and you have no other long-term gains this year. How much tax, in rupees, do you save by waiting, ignoring surcharge and cess?
body.explanation: Selling at 10 months: 20% of ₹1,50,000 = ₹30,000. Selling after 12 months: 12.5% of the gain above ₹1,25,000, which is 12.5% of ₹25,000 = ₹3,125. Waiting saves ₹26,875. That saving has to be weighed against the risk that the sector falls while you wait. A frequent rotation strategy that keeps crystallising short-term gains pays a heavy, recurring tax bill.

body.text: Tax rules change with Union Budgets, and your actual liability depends on your total income, other gains and losses, surcharge, and cess. Use the calculator for rough comparisons, and confirm your own position with a qualified tax adviser before acting.

children.text: Practice

body.title: The 80% Rule
body.textWithBlank: Under SEBI's categorisation rules, a sectoral or thematic mutual fund must invest at least ___% of its total assets in equities of its chosen sector or theme.
body.explanation: At least 80% must be in the sector or theme, which leaves the manager up to 20% for other holdings. From a February 2026 circular, sectoral and thematic funds are separate categories, and their overlap with other equity schemes is limited to 50%.

body.title: ETF Trading Trap
body.question: You want to buy a thinly traded sector ETF. Its indicative NAV is ₹100, but the best offer on the exchange is ₹103 and the best bid is ₹97. What is the main risk of buying at market?
options: There is no risk, because ETFs always trade at NAV
You would pay about 3% above the fund's underlying value, and might have to sell well below it later
The ETF will be delisted immediately
body.explanation: In an illiquid ETF, the traded price can sit well away from the indicative NAV. Buying at ₹103 against a value of about ₹100 costs you roughly 3% immediately, and selling into a ₹97 bid later could cost another 3%. That is many years' worth of a low expense ratio. Use limit orders, trade liquid ETFs, or consider the equivalent index fund instead.

cards.definition: The gap between a passive fund's return and its index's return, mainly caused by costs.
A near real-time estimate of an ETF's underlying value during market hours, used to judge whether the traded price is fair.
A charge, commonly around 1%, deducted if you redeem a mutual fund within a specified period.
From April 2026, the AMC's management fee component of total expenses, with brokerage and statutory levies shown separately.
A fund investing at least 80% in one sector. Separated from thematic funds, which can span two or more sectors, by SEBI in February 2026.
A gain on listed equity or equity-oriented funds held 12 months or less, taxed at 20% under Section 196 of the Income-tax Act, 2025.

body.title: Pick the Vehicle
body.scenario: Priya, a salaried professional in Pune, invests ₹25,000 a month through SIPs in a Nifty 50 index fund. After working through this course, she wants to add a tilt towards PSU banks, which her scorecard and relative strength analysis currently favour, using about 10% of her portfolio. She does not have time to research individual banks, and expects to review the tilt once or twice a year.
body.prompt: Which vehicle best suits Priya, and what should she check before starting?
body.modelAnswer: A low-cost sectoral index fund tracking the Nifty PSU Bank index is probably the best fit. It allows a monthly SIP alongside her existing investments, needs no stock research, and gives exactly the sector exposure her analysis points to. A PSU bank ETF is a reasonable alternative if she already has a demat account and the ETF trades with good volume and tight spreads, but an index fund avoids those trading checks. An active banking fund adds manager risk and higher costs without clearly serving her purpose, and direct stocks demand research she does not have time for. Before starting, she should compare expense ratios across available PSU bank index funds and ETFs, check the index's concentration in its largest banks, and plan her reviews so that, where possible, gains become long-term before she switches, since selling within 12 months would be taxed at 20% rather than 12.5% above the ₹1.25 lakh threshold.

body.text: This lesson is educational. Fund names are examples used to illustrate costs and structures, not recommendations. Expense ratios, exit loads, weights, and tax rules are as reported at the time of writing and will change. Consult a SEBI registered investment adviser and a qualified tax professional for decisions about your own portfolio.

points: The four ways to own a sector are index funds, ETFs, active sector or thematic funds, and direct stocks, each with different costs, concentration, and trading risks
Sector ETFs can have the lowest expense ratios, such as about 0.08% for the CPSE ETF, but thin trading and wide spreads can cost far more than the fee saved
Under SEBI rules, sectoral and thematic funds must invest at least 80% in their sector or theme, and a February 2026 circular separated the two categories
Sector indices are often top-heavy: TCS, Infosys, and HCL Technologies made up 68.75% of the Nifty IT index in July 2026
A 0.70 percentage point difference in annual costs can cost about ₹27,000 on ₹5 lakh over 5 years at a 12% gross return
Switching triggers capital gains tax: 20% on short-term equity gains, versus 12.5% on long-term gains above ₹1.25 lakh; on a ₹1.5 lakh gain, waiting past 12 months saves ₹26,875
Match the vehicle to how you invest: index funds for SIP tilts, liquid ETFs for lump sums, active funds for themes without an index, and stocks only for genuine company views
